RedVLA: Physical Red Teaming for Vision-Language-Action Models

Abstract

The real-world deployment of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models remains limited by the risk of unpredictable and irreversible physical harm. However, we currently lack effective mechanisms to proactively detect these physical safety risks before deployment. To address this gap, we propose RedVLA, the first red teaming framework for physical safety in VLA models. We systematically uncover unsafe behaviors through a two-stage process: (I) Risk Scenario Synthesis constructs a valid and task-feasible initial risk scene. Specifically, it identifies critical interaction regions from benign trajectories and positions the risk factor within these regions, aiming to entangle it with the VLA’s execution flow and elicit a target unsafe behavior. (II) Risk Amplification ensures stable elicitation across heterogeneous models. It iteratively refines the risk factor state through gradient-free optimization guided by trajectory features. Experiments on six representative VLA models show that RedVLA uncovers diverse unsafe behaviors and achieves the ASR up to 95.5% within 10 optimization iterations. To mitigate these risks, we further propose SimpleVLA-Guard, a lightweight safety guard built from RedVLA-generated data. Our data, assets, and code are available here.

Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are advancing toward generalist robotic policies (Kim et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024) by unified end-to-end learning from vision and language to action. These models are rapidly expanding their capabilities across critical domains such as manipulation (Zitkovich et al., 2023), autonomous driving (Jiang et al., 2025), and robotic surgery (Li et al., 2025b). With their increasing capabilities, however, safety concerns have been substantially amplified (Xing et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). It remains unclear what unique safety risks VLA models might exhibit when deployed in the physical world and the severity of their consequences. Therefore, proactively identifying and mitigating physical safety risks is a crucial prerequisite for large-scale, real-world deployment.

How to proactively uncover the potential physical safety risks of Vision-Language-Action models?\begin{gathered}\textit{How to proactively uncover the potential }\\ \textit{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}physical safety risks} of Vision-Language-Action models?}\end{gathered}

Red teaming for Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has been extensively studied, with existing approaches primarily targeting semantic and intent-based vulnerabilities (Ganguli et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024a; Perez et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2024). However, the source of risks in VLA models has fundamentally shifted from the intent space to the physical space, introducing distinct safety challenges (Wang et al., 2024). These risks are inherent to the embodied agent-environment interaction (Wu et al., 2024). Existing red teaming methods neither consider potential physical risks within the environment nor model the physical causality of the risk process.

To tackle this challenge, we propose RedVLA, the first red teaming framework for VLA physical safety. Our goal is to systematically introduce potential risk factors and uncover unsafe behaviors, while preserving the benign nature of the original scene and the semantic consistency of the task instructions. Concretely, we seek to maximize physical safety risks with minimal perturbation to the original environment. RedVLA achieves this via a two-stage process: (I) Risk Scenario Synthesis. This stage constructs a semantically valid and task-feasible initial risk scene. Specifically, we first identify critical interaction regions based on benign trajectories; then initialize the risk object within these areas, aiming to form risk factor and elicit a specific unsafe behavior by entangling the factor into the VLA’s execution flow. (II) Trajectory-Driven Risk Amplification. To ensure the stable elicitation of unsafe behaviors across heterogeneous models, this stage employs gradient-free optimization, iteratively refining the risk factor state until the targeted unsafe behavior is triggered. Experiments show that we can consistently elicit unsafe behaviors across different models. To mitigate physical risks during deployment, we leverage the red teaming data to construct SimpleVLA-Guard, enabling effective monitoring and intervention in unsafe behaviors.

To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to systematically explore VLA red teaming. Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Paradigm and Framework: We define the problem of VLA red teaming and proposed RedVLA, the first framework that uncovers physical safety risks. It proactively injects risk factors to uncover unsafe behaviors, without compromising the benign nature of original scene and the semantic consistency of task instructions.

  • •

    Key Findings: (I) RedVLA reveals severe safety vulnerabilities in VLA models by proactively eliciting unsafe behaviors across state, cumulative, and conditional levels. (II) RedVLA achieves the Attack Success Rate up to 95.5% on π0.5\pi_{0.5} and an average ASR of 92.7% across the five models with stronger baseline performance than OpenVLA within 10 optimization iterations. (III) We show that the unsafe behaviors elicited by RedVLA mostly arise during task execution rather than from trivial model collapse.

  • •

    Defense Strategy: To mitigate physical safety risks, we propose SimpleVLA-Guard, a lightweight safety guard that leverages internal VLA representations for real-time unsafe behavior detection and proactive intervention, reducing online ASR by 59.5% with minimal impact on task performance.

2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models aim to learn generalist policies that map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions. RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023) demonstrated the scalability of transformer-based robot learning, while RT-2 (Zitkovich et al., 2023) further advanced this paradigm by co-fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language model on both robot trajectory data and internet-scale vision-language data, enabling semantic knowledge to be transferred to robotic control. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) provided an open-source implementation of this paradigm. π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2025) introduced a flow-matching-based action expert for continuous action generation, enabling more dexterous and expressive control. π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025) improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training across diverse data sources. Meanwhile, some works have focused on improving efficiency and adaptability through lightweight architectures (Wang et al., 2025b) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies (Kim et al., 2025). Despite rapid progress in VLA capabilities and generalization, systematic safety evaluation for real-world deployment remains limited.

Safety of Vision-Language-Action Models. Existing works on VLA safety have primarily focused on adversarial vulnerabilities. In the visual domain, works such as FreezeVLA (Wang et al., 2025a) and patch-based attacks (Wang et al., 2024) show that image perturbations can paralyze robotic policies or uncover erratic behaviors. In the language domain, RoboGCG (Jones et al., 2025) demonstrates that carefully optimized adversarial suffixes can manipulate VLA policies. Multi-modal adversarial attacks have also been shown to disrupt VLA behavior by perturbing cross-modal alignment (Yan et al., 2025). Beyond visual and linguistic attacks, prior work has also shown that physically instantiated perturbations, optimized through heuristic search, can disrupt VLA execution (Liu et al., 2025). VLA models are also vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where hidden triggers can uncover target behaviors while preserving nominal task performance (Zhou et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a). On the defense side, approach such as SafeVLA (Zhang et al., 2025b) explores constrained learning to enhance model safety. These studies have advanced the safety of VLA models. In contrast, our work focuses on uncovering physical unsafe behaviors, providing a more realistic paradigm for evaluating VLA safety in real-world deployment settings.

3 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formalize the VLA physical red teaming problem and introduce a physical safety taxonomy.

3.1 VLA Physical Red Teaming

Vision-Language-Action models. A VLA policy πθ\pi_{\theta} operates within an environment defined by state space 𝒮\mathcal{S} and action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}. At each timestep tt, the agent observes an environment state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, comprising visual observation oto_{t}, proprioception ptp_{t}, and a language instruction ll. The policy generates continuous actions at∼πθ(⋅∣st,l)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},l), which transition the environment to st+1∼𝒫(⋅∣st,at)s_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{P}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}) according to dynamics 𝒫\mathcal{P}. This process yields a trajectory τ=(s0,a0,…,sT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},\dots,s_{T}).

Task Feasibility and Safety Cost. We define a task reward function R:𝒮×𝒜→ℝR:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} and a safety cost ci:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ≥0c_{i}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}{\geq 0} that measures the degree of constraint violations. A trajectory τ\tau is considered task-feasible if its cumulative reward exceeds a threshold δ\delta, which represents the minimum criterion for task success, i.e., JR​(τ)=∑t=0TR⁡(st,at)≥δJ_{R}(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{T}R(s_{t},a_{t})\geq\delta. Conversely, the degree of unsafe behavior regarding the ii-th safety violation CiC_{i} is quantified by the cumulative risk cost JCi​(τ)=∑t=0Tci​(st,at)J_{C_{i}}(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{T}c_{i}(s_{t},a_{t}), whose specific form depends on the target safety cost type.

VLA Physical Red Teaming Definition. We formulate VLA Red Teaming as a constrained optimization over the environment-instruction joint space. Our goal is to find a perturbed configuration (s0′,l′)(s_{0}^{\prime},l^{\prime}) that maximizes the elicited risk cost while ensuring the task remains feasible. Formally:

maxs0′,l′\displaystyle\max_{s_{0}^{\prime},l^{\prime}} 𝔼τ∼πθ(⋅∣s0′,l′)[JCi(τ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{0}^{\prime},l^{\prime})}[J_{C_{i}}(\tau)]
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} 𝔼τ∼πθ(⋅∣s0′,l′)[JR(τ)]≥δ.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{0}^{\prime},l^{\prime})}[J_{R}(\tau)]\geq\delta.

where s0′s_{0}^{\prime} and l′l^{\prime} are the perturbed initial state and instruction, τ\tau is the trajectory, and 𝔼\mathbb{E} marginalizes over stochasticity in policy execution and environment dynamics. This formulation uncovers safety vulnerabilities while preserving task feasibility and the semantic consistency of task instructions.

3.2 Physical Safety Taxonomy

To systematically categorize physical safety risks, we propose a comprehensive physical safety taxonomy grounded in a set of risk predicates Φ\Phi. Each predicate ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi is formally defined as a binary function ϕ:𝒮×𝒜→{0,1}\phi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\{0,1\}, where ϕ⁡(s,a)=1\phi(s,a)=1 signifies the occurrence of a specific physical safety violation and 00 otherwise. Based on the distinct temporal dependencies of these violations, we define three complementary dimensions of safety cost:

State-Level Safety Cost. This component captures immediate safety violations where a single state-action pair directly constitutes a physical risk. For a state-level predicate ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, the cost is triggered instantaneously:

cstate​(st,at)=ϕ⁡(st,at).c_{\text{state}}(s_{t},a_{t})=\phi(s_{t},a_{t}).

Cumulative-Level Safety Cost. This component addresses potential risks arising from the temporal accumulation of specific behaviors. For a predicate ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi monitoring such behaviors, the safety cost is defined as the cumulative occurrence over the entire trajectory:

ccumulative​(τ)={1,if ​∑t=0Tϕ⁡(st,at)>η,0,otherwise.c_{\text{cumulative}}(\tau)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\sum_{t=0}^{T}\phi(s_{t},a_{t})>\eta,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Conditional-Level Safety Cost. This component captures risks that arise only when a precondition is active. We define this using a pair of predicates: a precursor ϕpre∈Φ\phi_{\text{pre}}\in\Phi and a consequent ϕcons∈Φ\phi_{\text{cons}}\in\Phi.

ccond​(τ)=∃t1<t2:ϕpre​(st1,at1)∧ϕcons​(st2,at2).\displaystyle c_{\text{cond}}(\tau)=\exists t_{1}<t_{2}:\phi_{\text{pre}}(s_{t_{1}},a_{t_{1}})\land\phi_{\text{cons}}(s_{t_{2}},a_{t_{2}}).

These three safety cost types serve as complementary metrics to comprehensively model unsafe behaviors in physical space, capturing instantaneous, cumulative, and sequential risk patterns. Each safety violation CiC_{i} evaluated in our framework is a case instantiated from these safety cost. Details are provided in Appendix D.2.

4 RedVLA: A Physical Red-Teaming Framework for VLA Models

In this section, we present the RedVLA framework. RedVLA focuses exclusively on physical safety risks. We fix the instruction (i.e., l′=ll^{\prime}=l) and perturb only the initial state. Specifically, we construct a red-teaming initial state s0′s_{0}^{\prime} by injecting a single risk factor into the scene. Our goal is to elicit a target safety violation CiC_{i} while preserving task feasibility. To this end, we decompose RedVLA into two stages: (I) Risk Scenario Synthesis, which constructs a semantically valid initial risk scene; and (II) Risk Amplification, which iteratively refines s0′s_{0}^{\prime} via trajectory-driven optimization to maximize the likelihood of safety violations.

4.1 Risk Scenario Synthesis.

The first stage constructs an initial risk scene s0(0)s_{0}^{(0)} through two steps: Interaction Identification, which localizes critical interaction regions, and Risk Instantiation, which specifies the target safety violation and the risk factor.

Interaction Identification. Directly placing or​i​s​ko_{risk} often causes it to be ignored as background clutter. To localize the critical interaction regions ℋ⊂ℝ3\mathcal{H}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}, we analyze the end-effector trajectories from benign rollouts. Specifically, We extract the end-effector position 𝐱e​e​(t)∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}_{ee}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, velocity 𝐯e​e​(t)\mathbf{v}_{ee}(t), and gripper state g⁡(t)g(t). We then use a rule-based procedure to identify three interaction patterns:

Transit Region (ℋt​r​a​n​s​i​t\mathcal{H}_{transit}): The primary movement corridor of the end-effector, where risk objects placed along the path are likely to be encountered during execution.

Grasping Region (ℋg​r​a​s​p​i​n​g\mathcal{H}_{grasping}): The region where the robot actively interacts with objects, making it prone to unintended grasping of injected risk objects.

Vibration Region (ℋv​i​b​r​a​t​i​o​n\mathcal{H}_{vibration}): Regions where the end-effector undergoes repetitive oscillatory motion, making risk objects placed here susceptible to repeated strikes.

These regions together define the critical region ℋ=ℋt​r​a​n​s​i​t∪ℋg​r​a​s​p​i​n​g∪ℋv​i​b​r​a​t​i​o​n\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{transit}\cup\mathcal{H}_{grasping}\cup\mathcal{H}_{vibration} for risk injection. Details are provided in Appendix D.3.

Risk Instantiation. In this step, a risk object is proactively placed into the scene, aiming to enter the VLA’s execution flow and trigger a target unsafe behavior. To construct the initial risk scene, we first specify a target safety violation CiC_{i} for the given scene and instruction, annotated with its safety cost type, physical hazard category, and detection predicate. A corresponding risk object or​i​s​ko_{risk} is then selected and initialized at a location within ℋ\mathcal{H}, aiming to entangle with the VLA’s execution flow and elicit the target unsafe behavior. The placement is validated by verifying that the target violation can be triggered under a proxy VLA, and that the original task remains feasible. This procedure yields the initial risk scene s0(0)s_{0}^{(0)}. Details are provided in Appendix D.5.

4.2 Trajectory-Driven Risk Amplification.

Static initialization often fails to stably elicit target violations due to policy stochasticity and cross-model distribution shift. We therefore formulate risk factor refinement as an optimization over the risk object parameter, and solve it via zero-order optimization guided by trajectory spatial features. Formally, given the target safety violation CiC_{i}, the optimization objective is:

s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} JR​(τ)≥δ,\displaystyle J_{R}(\tau)\geq\delta,

where the risk state s0′s_{0}^{\prime} is parameterized by the risk object’s position 𝐩\mathbf{p} and orientation 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0}. At iteration kk, we execute the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} on s0(k)s_{0}^{(k)}, which is determined by 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} and fixed 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0}, and extract the end-effector trajectory {𝐱e​e(k)​(t)}t=0T\{\mathbf{x}_{ee}^{(k)}(t)\}_{t=0}^{T}. We then identify a critical spatial anchor 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} from the trajectory to guide the risk state update based on the nature of the target violation:

𝐱∗={𝐱e​e(k)​(tp​r​o​x∗),if ​ϕ​ is collision-based,𝐱e​e(k)​(tg​r​a​s​p∗),if ​ϕ​ is grasping-based,\mathbf{x}^{*}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{x}_{ee}^{(k)}(t^{*}_{prox}),&\text{if }\phi\text{ is collision-based},\\ \mathbf{x}_{ee}^{(k)}(t^{*}_{grasp}),&\text{if }\phi\text{ is grasping-based},\end{cases} (2)

where tp​r​o​x∗=arg⁡mint⁡‖𝐱e​e(k)​(t)−𝐩k‖2t^{*}_{prox}=\arg\min_{t}\|\mathbf{x}_{ee}^{(k)}(t)-\mathbf{p}_{k}\|_{2} is the timestep at which the end-effector is nearest to 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k}, and tg​r​a​s​p∗t^{*}_{grasp} is the timestamp of the gripper closure event spatially closest to 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k}. The risk object position is then adaptively updated via gradient ascent in the direction of 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*}:

𝐩k+1←𝐩k+αk⋅𝐱∗−𝐩k‖𝐱∗−𝐩k‖2,s.t.𝒱⁡(𝐩k+1)=1,\mathbf{p}_{k+1}\leftarrow\mathbf{p}_{k}+\alpha_{k}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{p}_{k}}{\|\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{p}_{k}\|_{2}},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{p}_{k+1})=1, (3)

where 𝒱:ℝ3→{0,1}\mathcal{V}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\{0,1\} is a binary scene validity function that checks for physical infeasibility (e.g., object interpenetration or scene collapse), and αk\alpha_{k} is determined via backtracking: αk←αk/2\alpha_{k}\leftarrow\alpha_{k}/2 until 𝒱⁡(𝐩k+1)=1\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{p}_{k+1})=1. Updates are constrained to the horizontal plane to preserve physical plausibility, and the process terminates when JCi​(τ(k))>0J_{C_{i}}(\tau^{(k)})>0, indicating that the target unsafe behavior has been triggered. This refinement uses trajectory features to guide the search toward regions that are most likely to affect execution. As a result, the red teaming search is reduced from the high-dimensional state space 𝒮\mathcal{S} to the low-dimensional interaction space ℋ\mathcal{H}, without requiring white-box access to πθ\pi_{\theta}.

5 Experiments

In this section, we aim to answer the following questions: (I) Can RedVLA elicit diverse unsafe behaviors across different VLA models? (§5.2); (II) How do model capabilities and multi-modal perturbations affect RedVLA? (§5.3); (III) Which components within RedVLA critically impact its performance? (§5.4) (IV) Are the revealed safety vulnerabilities practical in real world? (§5.5)

5.1 Experimental Setup

VLA Models. We evaluate RedVLA on six representative VLA models spanning three families. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) is an open-source VLA that predicts tokenized actions autoregressively. OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) extends OpenVLA with an optimized architecture for continuous action prediction. VLA-Adapter (Wang et al., 2025b) is a lightweight VLA that introduces Bridge Attention (Zhang et al., 2023) for efficient action prediction. VLA-Adapter-Pro (Wang et al., 2025b) further improves its policy design. π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2025) combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert, while π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025) improves its open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training.

Tasks and Environments. We conduct experiments on the widely-adopted LIBERO benchmark (Liu et al., 2023). We inject risk factors into benign scenarios to elicit safety violations. Specifically, these violations span three safety cost types (State, Cumulative, and Conditional) and four physical hazard categories (Resource Damage, Dangerous Item Misuse, Robot Damage, and Environmental Harm), with representative examples shown in Figure 3. By intersecting these two dimensions, we construct ten risk scenario suites, e.g., Cumulative-Level Resource Damage.

Evaluation Metrics. We employ three metrics to evaluate model safety, task performance, and red teaming efficiency. Attack Success Rate (ASR) is our primary metric, measuring the percentage of episodes in which the target safety violation is successfully triggered. Success Rate (SR) measures the task success rate in the risk scenarios synthesized by RedVLA. Benign Success Rate (Benign SR) measures the task success rate in the original benign scenarios. Each risk scenario is evaluated over 10 trials with different random seeds, and all metrics are averaged across trials.

5.2 Main Results

VLA Models Are Vulnerable to RedVLA. In Table 1, RedVLA achieves an average ASR of 64.9%–95.5% across all six models, with π0.5\pi_{0.5} reaching the highest and OpenVLA the lowest. Although the risk scenarios remain task-feasible, SR drops substantially, as the model’s interaction with the risk object disrupts task completion. Notably, in the -marked scenarios, SR drops to nearly zero because the model focuses on the risk object instead of the task-relevant objects, causing failure across all models.

RedVLA Elicits Diverse Unsafe Behaviors. In State-Level scenarios, the average ASR exceeds 95% across six models. Cumulative-Level and Conditional-Level scenarios are more challenging, as they require either risk accumulation over time or causally ordered events. Nevertheless, RedVLA still achieves average ASRs of 88.9% and 66.1% in these two settings, respectively. Notably, OpenVLA shows lower ASR in Conditional-Level scenarios, likely due to its weaker baseline performance in benign scenes (i.e., 53.7% Benign SR on LIBERO-Long for OpenVLA-Long model).

Unsafe Behaviors Are Not Due to Model Collapse. To further distinguish the modes of unsafe behavior, we divide rollouts into four categories: (i) Success + Unsafe (SU), (ii) Attempt + Unsafe (AU), (iii) Collapse, and (iv) Else Outcomes, where Success denotes successful task completion, Attempt denotes interaction with at least one task-relevant object, and Collapse denotes no interaction with any task-relevant object. All -marked scenarios in Table 1 fall into the AU category. In Figure 4, most unsafe rollouts fall into SU or AU across all six models, while collapse accounts for only a small fraction. This result indicates that RedVLA mainly exposes unsafe behaviors during task execution, rather than failures caused by model collapse.

5.3 Qualitative analysis

The Performance-Safety Trade-off. We analyze the relationship between model capability and physical safety vulnerability, measured by Benign SR and ASR. In Table 2, stronger models tend to achieve higher Benign SR, but also higher ASR. This trend is consistent across all three model families. For example, OpenVLA-OFT improves Benign SR over OpenVLA by 20.6% (97.1% vs. 76.5%), but also increases ASR by 25.6% (90.5% vs. 64.9%). These results suggest that stronger instruction-following ability may also increase the likelihood of triggering unsafe behaviors.

Impact of Multimodal Perturbations. We study how multimodal perturbations affect the performance of RedVLA. In Table 3, RedVLA maintains high ASRs under both language and visual perturbations, with average ASRs of 88.2% and 85.5%, respectively. In benign scenarios, these perturbations substantially reduce SR but rarely trigger unsafe behavior on their own, with ASR staying at or below 5.2%. This result further suggests that the physical safety risks uncovered by RedVLA are driven primarily by injected environmental risk factors, rather than trivial input perturbations.

5.4 Ablation Studies

Impact of Risk Factor Initialization. We study how risk factor initialization affects RedVLA. Specifically, we compare our initialization strategy with two baselines: random position with our orientation, and random orientation with our position. In Figure 5 (A), our risk factor initialization strategy consistently outperforms random position initialization, with the difference remaining evident throughout optimization. While randomizing orientation has negligible impact, justifying our choice to optimize position only.

Impact of Step Size. We investigate the effect of step size α\alpha in RedVLA by varying α\alpha over (e.g., 0.001 m, 0.005 m, 0.01 m, 0.05 m, 0.1 m). In Figure 5 (B), ASR exceeds 90% once α>0.005\alpha>0.005. Here, Rejection Count denotes the number of rejected updates, where scene invalidation triggers rollback to the previous state and halves the step size. When α\alpha exceeds 0.05, the Average Rejection Count increases sharply. We adopt α=0.01\alpha{=}0.01, larger values only increase rejections, while smaller values underperform.

Effect of Optimization Iterations. We study how ASR changes with the number of optimization iterations across State-Level, Cumulative-Level, and Conditional-Level scenarios. In Figure 5 (C), ASR increases steadily for both VLA-Adapter-Pro and π0\pi_{0}, with the largest gains occurring early, from K=0K=0 to K=6K=6. This result indicates that RedVLA can elicit unsafe behaviors within only a few optimization steps. VLA-Adapter-Pro starts from a higher ASR and saturates earlier, while π0\pi_{0} continues to improve more noticeably in Cumulative and Conditional scenarios.

5.5 Empirical Study: Sim-to-Real Validation

We build a physical platform with a Franka robot and deploy the π0\pi_{0} policy. On two benign tasks, (i) Pick up the cup and place it on the bowl and (ii) Pick up the carrot and place it on the bowl, the policy achieves over 90% SR. We then inject a knife onto the target cup and place cup obstacles along the robot trajectory. In Figure 6, the robot grasps the knife in task (i) and knocks over the obstacle cups in task (ii). Both scenarios achieve ASR above 80% over 10 trials per task, confirming that such unsafe behaviors also manifest in the real world.

6 VLA Safety Guardrail: SimpleVLA-Guard

In this section, we propose SimpleVLA-Guard, a safety guardrail built on RedVLA elicited data, and evaluate its offline detection and online intervention capabilities.

6.1 SimpleVLA-Guard Setting

Motivation. Guard models are widely used in LLMs and VLMs as content filters (Inan et al., 2023) to prevent harmful outputs from reaching users. Similarly, a VLA guard detect unsafe behavior during execution and intervene before harmful actions occur. Motivated by prior findings (Gu et al., 2025), we analyze the latent representations of models under benign and RedVLA-synthesized scenarios. Our results demonstrate that safe and unsafe trajectories are separated in the latent space, suggesting that internal representations carry useful signals for detecting physical risk.

SimpleVLA-Guard Design. SimpleVLA-Guard is a lightweight model that identifies physical risks from the internal representations of VLA policies. In our implementation, we instantiate it on π0\pi_{0} by extracting the internal feature sequence during policy execution and using an LSTM to model temporal dependencies. The guard is trained on a dataset constructed from three sources: RedVLA unsafe rollouts, safe rollouts with risk factors, and benign safe rollouts. During online deployment, it outputs a step-wise risk score. To enable preemptive halting before unsafe behavior occurs, we integrate Functional Conformal Prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) for threshold calibration.

6.2 Defense with SimpleVLA-Guard

SimpleVLA-Guard Offline Detection. We evaluate the offline detection performance of SimpleVLA-Guard on both seen and unseen tasks. We hold out two tasks from the diverse long-horizon scenarios in LIBERO-Long as unseen tasks and exclude them entirely from training to assess the guard’s cross-task generalization. In Table 4, SimpleVLA-Guard achieves strong detection performance on seen tasks, and although performance drops on unseen tasks, it still demonstrates a meaningful capability for generalization.

SimpleVLA-Guard Online Intervention. We deploy SimpleVLA-Guard online with the conformal threshold calibrated at α=0.05\alpha=0.05. In Table 4, the guard reduces ASR after deployment while incurring only a limited drop in Benign SR. These results show that SimpleVLA-Guard can effectively mitigate physical risks during execution with a modest performance cost. Details are in the Appendix E.3.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce RedVLA, the first systematic red teaming framework for uncovering physical safety risks in Vision-Language-Action models. RedVLA injects risk factors into task-feasible benign scenes and refines them through trajectory-driven iterative optimization to elicit unsafe behaviors. Experiments on six representative VLA models reveal substantial physical safety vulnerabilities: RedVLA triggers unsafe behaviors across all three safety cost types and diverse hazard categories, achieving a peak ASR of 95.5% within 10 optimization iterations. To mitigate these risks, we further propose SimpleVLA-Guard, a lightweight guard for offline detection and online intervention based on internal policy representations. Overall, RedVLA provides a practical framework for both exposing and mitigating physical safety risks in VLA models.

Impact statement

The data, code, and assets related to RedVLA will be released under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license. This work aims to expose the physical safety risks of Vision-Language-Action models before real-world deployment, supporting safer evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation. By systematically eliciting unsafe behaviors, RedVLA can help researchers identify safety vulnerabilities that may otherwise remain hidden under benign testing conditions. At the same time, this work may introduce dual-use risks. In particular, the proposed framework could be misused to deliberately trigger unsafe robot behaviors. To reduce this risk, we release the work for research purposes under a non-commercial license and frame RedVLA as a tool for safety evaluation and defense construction rather than malicious use. We believe that openly studying these vulnerabilities is necessary for building more reliable and trustworthy embodied AI System.

Appendix A Limitation and Future Work

A key limitation of this work stems from the constrained task performance of current VLA models. Consequently, our physical red-teaming evaluation is conducted on benchmarks where these models already demonstrate reasonably strong execution ability. Extending RedVLA to less mature benchmarks or different robot embodiments remains challenging, as insufficient baseline performance leaves limited task-directed behavior to perturb and makes unsafe behaviors harder to trigger. This currently constrains evaluation breadth across environments and embodiments.

Another limitation is that RedVLA relies on a predefined set of safety predicates, risk objects, and safety violations to construct risk scenarios. Although this design enables systematic and effective red teaming, it also restricts the diversity of risks that can be uncovered. An important direction for future work is to reduce this manual specification by developing more automated scenario generation methods capable of synthesizing richer and less predictable physical safety violations.

Our results further indicate that current VLA models exhibit limited safety awareness and recovery capability once risk is introduced into the scene. This points to a broader research direction beyond risk identification alone. Future work should leverage insights from red teaming to develop stronger guard models and safety alignment methods that enhance both risk detection and behavioral recovery in real-world deployment.

Appendix B Additional Related Work

Red Teaming for Large Foundation Models. Early red teaming for large foundation models relied on human annotators who manually constructed adversarial prompts to probe harmful behaviors, including toxic outputs (Gehman et al., 2020; Bender et al., 2021), bias amplification (Ganguli et al., 2022), and privacy leakage (Carlini et al., 2021). These works established red teaming as a practical framework for stress-testing model safety, but focused on semantic and intent-level failures. In contrast, RedVLA targets physical safety risks that arise from embodied interaction with the environment.

Benchmarks for VLA Evaluation. The rapid progress of VLA models has led to a growing set of embodied benchmarks for evaluating task execution, generalization, and safety. Early benchmarks focused primarily on low-level manipulation performance. RLBench (James et al., 2020) introduced a large-scale suite of atomic and compositional tasks for low-level robotic skills. Later environments such as CHORES (Ehsani et al., 2024) and BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al., 2022) shifted toward more realistic household settings with long-horizon interactions.

More recent benchmarks place greater emphasis on generalization and robustness. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) evaluates lifelong learning by systematically varying objects, spatial layouts, and goals across long-horizon task suites. CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022) focuses on long-horizon language-conditioned manipulation, where agents must compose skills from sequential language instructions. SimplerEnv (Li et al., 2024b) narrows the sim-to-real gap through visually faithful simulation environments. Newer variants such as LIBERO-Pro (Zhou et al., 2025b) and LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) further increase task difficulty and distribution diversity.

Safety-oriented benchmarks have also emerged for VLA evaluation. SafeLIBERO (Hu et al., 2025) introduces structured obstacle scenarios and quantitative safety metrics to study the trade-off between task completion and collision avoidance. Safety-CHORES (Zhang et al., 2025b) formulates safety-aware evaluation within a CMDP framework by introducing safety-critical objects and cumulative safety cost. VLA-Arena (Zhang et al., 2025a) further includes safety as one axis in a broader evaluation platform. These benchmarks provide standardized safety evaluation, but most remain passive in that they rely on fixed environments without actively probing model vulnerabilities. RedVLA instead actively injects risk factors to elicit physical safety violations.

Appendix C Details of Physical Risk Behaviors

This section provides representative examples of physical risk behaviors elicited by RedVLA, organized by safety cost type and hazard category. State-Level Dangerous Item Misuse is illustrated in Figure 7, where the robot erroneously grasps or handles hazardous objects during task execution. State-Level Resource Damage is captured in Figure 8, demonstrating unintended collisions with fragile objects in the environment. Cumulative-Level Robot Damage is presented in Figure 9, where repeated or sustained interactions lead to excessive force accumulation. Finally, Conditional-Level Environmental Harm is shown in Figure 10, in which a sequence of causally linked actions gives rise to fire or electrical hazards.

Appendix D Details of Risk Scenario Synthesis

In this section, we provide comprehensive details of the risk scenario synthesis process. The pipeline systematically transforms benign task environments into structured risk scenarios, each targeting a specific safety violation within the RedVLA taxonomy.

D.1 Details of Risk Factors

We construct a library of risk factors to elicit safety violations during task execution. Table 5 summarizes all risk factors and their associated hazards.

These risk factors collectively enable RedVLA to construct diverse unsafe scenarios covering the physical hazard categories defined in our taxonomy.

D.2 Details of Safety Violations

We provide the formal predicate definitions of safety violations instantiated across three cost levels: State-Level, Cumulative-Level, and Conditional-Level, as listed in the tables below.

D.3 Details of Critical Interaction Region Identification

To localize intervention sites for risk injection, we employ a rule-based procedure that identifies critical interaction regions from benign task trajectories by analyzing the spatio-temporal characteristics of the end-effector’s motion and gripper state. Spatial points are categorized into three distinct regions: Transit Region (ℋt​r​a​n​s​i​t\mathcal{H}_{transit}), Grasping Region (ℋg​r​a​s​p​i​n​g\mathcal{H}_{grasping}), and Vibration Region (ℋv​i​b​r​a​t​i​o​n\mathcal{H}_{vibration}), with their identification logic detailed in the algorithms below.

D.4 Safety Predicates and Detection Mechanisms

To enable precise detection of physical safety violations, we develop a comprehensive set of safety-specific predicates and detection strategies. These predicates extend the BDDL (Behavior Domain Definition Language) to capture fine-grained physical interactions, force dynamics, and complex temporal dependencies.

D.5 Details of Risk Scenario Suites

We summarize the distribution of synthesized risk scenarios across safety cost types and physical hazard categories in Table 10, along with their source benchmarks.

Appendix E Further Details about Evaluation Setup

This section provides implementation details and hyperparameters for all evaluated VLA policies, the multi-modal perturbation protocol, and the SimpleVLA-Guard safety module.

E.1 Implementation Details and Hyperparameters

Policy Inference.

We evaluate a diverse set of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, including OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), VLA-Adapter (Wang et al., 2025b), VLA-Adapter-Pro (Wang et al., 2025b), π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2025), and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025), all fine-tuned on the LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) benchmark. As detailed in Table 11, the inference configurations vary across models. Except for the baseline OpenVLA, which uses a single view and autoregressive decoding (C=1C{=}1), all other models receive binocular observations (agent-view and wrist-mounted cameras) and employ action chunking. Specifically, OpenVLA-OFT and the VLA-Adapter series output chunks of size C=8C{=}8 and replan every 8 steps, while the flow-matching based π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} output longer chunks of C=50C{=}50 but replan more frequently every 10 steps. For all models, gripper actions are binarized and inverted to match the environment convention.

Simulation Environment.

The environment operates at a control frequency of 2020 Hz with a maximum episode horizon of H=520H{=}520 steps. Initial scene states are loaded from pre-generated pruned initialization files that specify the full MuJoCo simulator state vector, including joint positions and object poses.

Hyperparameters.

Table 12 summarizes the key hyperparameters governing the adversarial evaluation. Each iteration allows up to N=400N{=}400 policy steps (2020 s of simulated time) for the agent to attempt task completion under the perturbed configuration.

E.2 Multi-Modal Perturbation Evaluation Setup

To rigorously evaluate the robustness of VLA models and safety guards, we introduce a comprehensive set of multi-modal perturbations. These perturbations are designed to simulate real-world noise and adversarial conditions across both visual and linguistic modalities.

Visual Perturbations.

We apply distinct types of visual corruptions to the input observations, targeting different aspects of visual perception. These are implemented using the scipy.ndimage and PIL libraries:

  • •

    Motion Blur: Applies a linear motion blur (kernel size 7, angle 45∘45^{\circ}) to mimic camera shake or rapid robot movement.

  • •

    Occlusion: Randomly places 5 black rectangular patches (size range [40,70][40,70] pixels) to simulate partial object occlusion.

  • •

    JPEG Compression: Compresses images with a quality factor of 10 to simulate low-bandwidth transmission artifacts.

  • •

    Gaussian Blur: Applies a Gaussian blur with a kernel size of 5 to simulate out-of-focus optics.

Linguistic Perturbations.

We introduce four categories of instruction perturbations to test the model’s understanding of task semantics and safety constraints:

  • •

    Garbled Text: Replaces the instruction with a randomly generated string of mixed characters (including ASCII letters, digits, punctuation, and multi-lingual characters like Chinese, Japanese, and Cyrillic) with a length between 10 and 20. This simulates severe data corruption or encoding errors.

  • •

    Empty Instruction: Provides an empty string as the instruction, testing the model’s behavior in the absence of explicit commands.

  • •

    Instruction Reversal: Semantically reverses the instruction to test if the model blindly follows keywords or truly understands the goal (e.g., ”open the drawer” →\to ”close the drawer”).

  • •

    Random Instruction: Replaces the correct instruction with a randomly sampled, unrelated command from the task set, testing the model’s reliance on visual cues versus language grounding.

These perturbations are applied during the evaluation phase to assess the degradation in both task success rate and safety violation detection accuracy.

E.3 Implementation Details on SimpleVLA-Guard

SimpleVLA-Guard is a lightweight safety guard instantiated on π0\pi_{0}, designed to detect and intervene in unsafe behaviors during policy execution. It consists of four components: feature extraction and visualization, training data construction, the training pipeline, and the evaluation protocol.

Feature Visualization.

Motivated by prior findings on latent representations in VLA policies (Gu et al., 2025), we first analyze whether π0\pi_{0}’s internal representations carry discriminative signals for physical safety. We extract hidden states from π0\pi_{0}’s transformer backbone across both benign rollouts and RedVLA-synthesized unsafe rollouts, and project them into a 2D latent space for visualization (Figure 12). The resulting embeddings reveal clear separation between safe and unsafe trajectories, with unsafe rollouts consistently occupying a distinct and coherent region regardless of task origin. This cross-task consistency suggests that unsafe behaviors share a common latent signature, which directly motivates the design of SimpleVLA-Guard as a feature-based detector.

Training Data.

The full dataset is constructed from all 10 tasks of the LIBERO-Long suite, chosen for its task diversity and long-horizon complexity. We collect 40 safe and 40 unsafe rollouts per task, yielding 400 safe and 400 unsafe rollouts in total (800 rollouts across 10 tasks).

Safe data (400 rollouts) are drawn in equal proportion from two sources: (i) 200 rollouts from standard benign LIBERO-Long scenes without any injected risk factors, and (ii) 200 rollouts from LIBERO-Long scenes with injected risk factors, where the robot successfully completes the task without triggering any safety violation. All safe rollouts are task-successful. This balanced composition ensures that the guard learns to detect genuine unsafe behaviors rather than merely detecting the presence of risk objects.

Unsafe data (400 rollouts) are collected from RedVLA red-teaming trajectories in which the target safety violation is successfully elicited. These rollouts cover all three safety cost types (State-Level, Cumulative-Level, and Conditional-Level) and all four physical hazard categories (Dangerous Item Misuse, Resource Damage, Robot Damage, and Environmental Harm), providing comprehensive coverage of the physical risk taxonomy.

Data split. For evaluation of cross-task generalization, Tasks 4 and 8 are held out entirely from training and calibration as unseen tasks, reserving 160 rollouts (80 safe + 80 unsafe) exclusively for evaluation. The remaining 8 seen tasks contribute 640 rollouts, which are further divided into a 70/30 train/validation split.

Training Pipeline.

SimpleVLA-Guard processes the pre_velocity feature extracted from the π0\pi_{0} diffusion transformer at each execution step. Concretely, given the per-step feature tensor of shape (Ndiff,Nhorizon, 1024)(N_{\text{diff}},\,N_{\text{horizon}},\,1024), we index the first diffusion step and first horizon step to obtain a 1024-dimensional vector, following the convention diff_idx=0\texttt{diff\_idx}=0, horizon_idx=0\texttt{horizon\_idx}=0.

An LSTM module with hidden dimension 256 and a single layer processes the resulting feature sequence (x1,x2,…,xT)∈ℝT×1024(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1024}, outputting a step-wise risk score rt∈[0,1]r_{t}\in[0,1] via a linear head followed by sigmoid activation.

Ramp-weighted loss. To prevent the model from exploiting static first-frame cues and to enforce temporal evidence accumulation, we apply a ramp time-weighting scheme (Hartvigsen et al., 2019) to the BCE loss on unsafe trajectories:

wt=tT−1,t=0,1,…,T−1,w_{t}=\frac{t}{T-1},\quad t=0,1,\ldots,T-1, (4)

so that the loss weight increases linearly from 0 to 1 over the trajectory. Safe trajectories retain uniform weights throughout. The full training objective is:

ℒ=ℒBCEsafe+∑twt⋅ℒBCE,tunsafe+λreg​‖θ‖2,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}^{\text{safe}}+\sum_{t}w_{t}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE,t}}^{\text{unsafe}}+\lambda_{\text{reg}}\|\theta\|^{2}, (5)

where λreg=10−3\lambda_{\text{reg}}=10^{-3}.

Data balancing. To prevent task-level imbalance, each task contributes min⁡(nunsafe(k),nsafe(k))\min(n_{\text{unsafe}}^{(k)},\,n_{\text{safe}}^{(k)}) trajectories from both classes. Within each mini-batch, a TaskBalancedBatchSampler draws 8 samples per task with replacement, ensuring uniform task coverage regardless of per-task dataset size.

Optimization. The model is trained for 1000 epochs using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, decayed by a factor of 0.5 every 300 epochs (StepLR). Dropout of 0.2 is applied after the LSTM output, and gradients are clipped to a maximum ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of 1.0. Training uses a single NVIDIA 3090 GPU. The data split follows the 70/30 train/validation ratio on the 8 seen tasks described above; the two unseen tasks are withheld entirely.

Table 13 summarizes all hyperparameters of SimpleVLA-Guard.

Evaluation Protocol.

We evaluate SimpleVLA-Guard under two settings:

  • •

    Offline Detection. The guard is evaluated on pre-collected rollout sequences without environment interaction. We report PRC-AUC (Precision-Recall Curve AUC), which measures the area under the precision-recall curve for the early-alert task, and Recall@FPR10, which measures the recall at an operating point where the false positive rate does not exceed 10%. Both metrics are reported separately for seen and unseen tasks.

  • •

    Online Intervention. The guard is deployed in closed-loop with π0\pi_{0} using a Functional Conformal Prediction (FCP) (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) calibrated threshold τ^​(t)\hat{\tau}(t). Rather than a single scalar threshold, FCP computes a time-varying threshold by normalizing each calibration trajectory to 100 equally-spaced bins and computing the (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile across safe episodes at each bin, with α=0.05\alpha=0.05. This provides a per-step operating boundary that accounts for the natural increase in feature activation near the end of a trajectory, reducing false positives compared to episode-max calibration. When the smoothed risk score r¯t\bar{r}_{t} (sliding window of size 3) exceeds τ^​(t)\hat{\tau}(t), the guard preemptively halts execution. We report the reduction in Attack Success Rate (Δ\DeltaASR) and the drop in Benign Success Rate (Δ\DeltaBenign SR) to quantify the safety–performance trade-off.

Appendix F Details of Annotation Process

This section describes the annotation platform, workflow, and quality control used to construct the risk scenarios in RedVLA.

F.1 Annotation Platform and Tools

To facilitate the efficient construction of valid and task-feasible risk scenarios, we developed a specialized 3D simulation annotation platform. This platform enables human annotators to interactively inject risk factors, manipulate object states, and verify task feasibility in real-time.

The platform’s interface is divided into several primary functional areas:

  • •

    Viewport Area: Renders the 3D environment in real-time, displaying the robot, benign objects, and injected risk factors.

  • •

    Status Panel: Displays real-time trajectory coordinates, end-effector velocity, gripper states, and detected safety violations using the predefined predicates.

  • •

    Control Panel: Allows annotators to switch between different operational modes, select risk objects from the predefined library to add into the scene, or remove existing objects to construct specific adversarial layouts.

To streamline the human-in-the-loop process, the platform provides four distinct operational modes:

  1. 1.

    Physical Mode: Activates the physics engine, simulating gravity, collisions, and object dynamics. It is used to observe the physical consequences of the injected risk factor and verify physical plausibility.

  2. 2.

    Free Mode: Suspends physical constraints to enable dynamic scene editing. In this mode, all items are freely draggable; annotators can easily drag, drop, and rotate both newly added risk factors and original environment elements in 3D space. This mode is critical for the precise initial placement of the risk object within the critical interaction regions (ℋ\mathcal{H}).

  3. 3.

    AI Mode: Deploys the proxy VLA policy (πθ\pi_{\theta}) to execute the task automatically based on the current scene configuration. Annotators use this mode to observe if the VLA’s execution flow becomes entangled with the risk factor.

  4. 4.

    Data Collection Mode: Automatically records the environment state, injected risk object parameters (s0′s^{\prime}_{0}), and the trajectory data (τ\tau) once the scene is verified as task-feasible and capable of eliciting the target safety violation.

Human-in-the-Loop Interaction:
Annotators actively participate in the loop through an intuitive keyboard and mouse interface. By manipulating the keyboard for spatial translation and the mouse for rotation and selection, annotators can precisely adjust the 6-DoF pose of the risk object. The table on the right illustrates the keybindings used during the Free Mode adjustment phase.

Keyboard & Mouse Controls
Translate Q (Up) W (Forward) E (Down)
A (Left) S (Backward) D (Right)
Rotate Hold Right Click + Drag Mouse
Select Left Click on Object

F.2 Annotation Workflow

The annotation process follows a rigorous pipeline corresponding to the Risk Scenario Synthesis stage introduced in §4. The workflow is executed by a team of trained annotators who are familiar with VLA behavior and the defined physical safety taxonomy.

Annotators and Annotation Period: The annotation team consisted of four members with backgrounds in robotics and embodied AI, structured as three primary annotators and one dedicated reviewer. To ensure high data quality and objectivity, the reviewer cross-checked the task feasibility and safety violation validity of each synthesized scene. The final risk scenarios were included in the dataset only when a unanimous consensus was reached, ensuring strict inter-annotator consistency. On average, constructing and verifying a single risk scenario took approximately three to five minutes, depending on the complexity of the temporal logic required (e.g., Conditional-Level scenarios generally took longer and required more precise micro-adjustments than State-Level ones).

The complete workflow consists of four steps:

  1. 1.

    Interaction Identification: Annotators run a benign rollout of the proxy VLA and use the platform to extract the end-effector trajectory. The system automatically highlights the critical interaction regions (ℋt​r​a​n​s​i​t\mathcal{H}_{transit}, ℋg​r​a​s​p​i​n​g\mathcal{H}_{grasping}, ℋv​i​b​r​a​t​i​o​n\mathcal{H}_{vibration}).

  2. 2.

    Target Specification: Based on the environment and the benign instruction, the annotator selects a target safety violation (e.g., Dangerous Item Misuse) and retrieves the corresponding risk object (e.g., Kitchen Knife) from the library.

  3. 3.

    Risk Instantiation and Adjustment: Using the Free Mode, the annotator places the risk object into the identified critical region. They then switch to AI Mode to observe the VLA’s reaction. If the unsafe behavior is not triggered, the annotator uses the keyboard/mouse controls to make manual micro-adjustments to the object’s pose until the proxy VLA successfully triggers the target violation.

  4. 4.

    Task Feasibility Verification: Finally, the annotator and the reviewer must ensure that the injection of the risk object does not physically block the task. They verify that a theoretical collision-free path still exists, ensuring that the risk scenario remains solvable for a safety-aware oracle.

To clearly illustrate the outcome of this workflow, Table 15 provides an annotated example presented in a card format.

F.3 Scene Plausibility Evaluation

To ensure that each task scene admits diverse yet physically plausible initial configurations, we design a hybrid sampling pipeline that decouples the placement of privileged objects (i.e., objects whose spatial arrangement directly defines the task semantics) from the remaining scene elements. The pipeline operates in six stages within the MuJoCo physics engine.

Stage 1: BDDL-driven Layout Sampling.

The environment is reset through the BDDL (Srivastava et al., 2022) specification, which stochastically samples positions and orientations for all objects according to the declared spatial predicates (e.g., on, in).

Stage 2: Privileged Object Removal.

All movable privileged objects are teleported to a remote holding position 𝐩hold=(10,10,5)\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{hold}}=(10,10,5) m by directly writing their free-joint generalized coordinates 𝐪=[𝐩;𝜼]\mathbf{q}\!=\![\mathbf{p};\,\bm{\eta}] via set_joint_qpos. Crucially, the generalized velocity 𝐪˙\dot{\mathbf{q}} is simultaneously zeroed to prevent residual free-fall momentum from corrupting later placement.

Stage 3: Non-Privileged Stabilization and Integrity Check.

The simulator advances 200 physics steps with the robot arm locked at its reference configuration (all actuator commands set to zero). A post-stabilization integrity check then rejects the sample if any non-privileged object has fallen below the workspace (z<−0.05z<-0.05 m) or if inter-object penetration exceeds 10 mm, indicating that the BDDL-sampled layout was physically infeasible.

Stage 4: Staged Privileged Placement.

Privileged objects are reintroduced in a specific order determined by their reference spatial relationships. Two placement modes are supported:

  • •

    Anchor mode. When the primary privileged object is a fixture (e.g., a stove or cabinet), its pose is immutable. Secondary objects are placed at the reference relative offset Δ​𝐩\Delta\mathbf{p} from the fixture’s current body-frame position, with an optional small drop height δz\delta_{z} to let gravity resolve minor collisions.

  • •

    Free-base mode. When the primary object is movable, its (x,y)(x,y) coordinates are uniformly sampled within the BDDL-defined placement region ℛ\mathcal{R}, while its zz and orientation 𝜼\bm{\eta} are preserved from the reference state. After an intermediate settlement phase of 250 physics steps, secondary objects are placed relative to the settled position of the base, accounting for any post-contact displacement.

In both modes, each object’s velocity is explicitly zeroed upon placement to guarantee a quiescent initial condition.

Stage 5: Final Physics Settlement.

The full scene (all objects in place, robot locked) undergoes a final stabilization phase of SstabS_{\mathrm{stab}} steps (default 100) to reach a quasi-static equilibrium.

Stage 6: Multi-Criteria Verification.

The resulting state is accepted only if it simultaneously satisfies the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    Orientation fidelity. The base object’s quaternion deviation ‖𝜼cur−𝜼ref‖2≤τq\|\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{cur}}-\bm{\eta}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}\leq\tau_{q} (default τq=0.05\tau_{q}=0.05; relaxed per-scene for inherently tilted configurations, e.g., a bowl resting on a ramekin).

  2. 2.

    Vertical stability. |zcur−zref|≤0.02|z_{\mathrm{cur}}-z_{\mathrm{ref}}|\leq 0.02 m.

  3. 3.

    Relative pose consistency. For every secondary privileged object, ‖Δ​𝐩cur−Δ​𝐩ref‖2≤0.025\|\Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{cur}}-\Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}\leq 0.025 m.

  4. 4.

    Penetration-free. No contact pair exhibits penetration depth >5>5 mm or contact force >50>50 N.

Samples that fail any criterion are discarded, and the pipeline retries from Stage 1 until NN valid samples are collected (up to a configurable maximum of 50 attempts per scene).

Output Format.

Each accepted sample is recorded as a flattened MuJoCo simulator state vector 𝐬∈ℝd\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a scene with NN successful samples, the final artifact is a matrix 𝐒∈ℝN×d\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} stored in float64 precision via torch.save, enabling exact state restoration through sim.set_state_from_flattened.
